name: The Tinderbox
powers: Striking it summons three dogs that fetch treasure, a princess, and rescue from prison.
description: The magic flint and tinder of Hans Christian Andersen's tale, in which a soldier finds an old witch's tinderbox in a hollow tree guarded by three enormous dogs. Each strike of the flint summons one of the dogs, which bring him money, the princess, and rescue from prison. The story, built on older folk motifs of the magic object, turned the homely tinderbox into the key to wealth and a kingdom.

name: The Flying Trunk
powers: Carries its owner through the air to wherever he wishes.
description: The enchanted wooden trunk of Andersen's tale, given to a spendthrift merchant's son by a rich merchant and used by its owner to fly to the land of the Turks and court a princess. When he squanders his last coins on fireworks, the sparks set the trunk alight and it burns to ash, leaving him to wander. The tale plays the magic object as both luck and ruin.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, Den flyvende kuffert (1839)

name: The Magic Book
powers: Grants knowledge, secrets, or magical skill to whoever reads it.
description: A book endowed with supernatural power in the Danish tale of the same name, granting its owner knowledge, hidden secrets, or magical skill, and bringing both power and danger. Magic books of this kind echo the real black books of Scandinavian folk magic, which were used to heal and to find lost things. The story belongs to the Nordic cycle of grimoire legends.
source: Danish folk tale, collected in tale collections

name: The Red Shoes
powers: The shoes make their wearer dance, without rest, wherever she goes.
description: The enchanted red shoes of Andersen's tale of Karen, a proud village girl who wants shoes finer than her station. Once she puts on the red shoes they carry her dancing uncontrollably, over thorns and across the country, until she has the axe cut them from her feet and repents. The tale, rooted in village dress codes, made fine shoes a symbol of vanity punished.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, De røde sko (1845)

name: The Snow Queen's Mirror
powers: Reflects everything good and fair as mean and ugly; splinters pierce the heart and eye.
description: The devil's magic mirror from the first chapter of Andersen's 'The Snow Queen'. It magnifies everything ugly and shrinks all that is good, and when the trolls drop it, it shatters into millions of splinters. Splinters blown into the eyes and hearts of the children Kay and Gerda set the story in motion, for Kay's changed vision is what lets the Snow Queen take him away.

name: The Tallow Candle
powers: Burns with a clear flame when it finds its purpose.
description: The tallow candle of a Danish poem credited to a young Hans Christian Andersen and found in the national archive in 2012. In the poem a rough, unlit candle complains that it has never burned, until it finds its true use and gives light. The discovery pushed the start of Andersen's literary career back to the early 1820s, and the poem is treated as his earliest known work.

name: The Steadfast Tin Soldier
material: Tin, cast from an old tin spoon
powers: Falls from the window, rides a paper boat, and is swallowed by a fish, yet never bends.
description: The one-legged toy soldier of Andersen's tale, cast last from the family's old tin spoon and brave out of all proportion. Sailing his paper boat through the gutter and burned at last in the stove with the paper dancer he loved, he never flinches. The tale made the plain tin soldier a figure of quiet constancy and one of Andersen's most loved objects.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, Den standhaftige tinsoldat (1838)

name: The Jelling Stones
powers: King Harald's runes proclaim that he won Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.
description: The two great runestones of the royal monument at Jelling, Jutland, raised by kings Gorm and Harald Bluetooth in the 10th century. Harald's stone, carved with the oldest portrait of Christ in Denmark, announces that he 'won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian', marking Denmark's conversion. The stones stand in the churchyard as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

name: The Danevirke
description: A system of ramparts, walls, and moats running across the base of Jutland at Schleswig, built from the 5th century onward to guard the southern border of Denmark. It was manned and rebuilt at many points in its history and is described in the English royal chronicle of Æthelweard. The surviving stretches are a UNESCO World Heritage site, partly preserved under the modern border.

name: The Black Book (Sortebog)
powers: Used by cunning folk to heal the sick, find stolen goods, and undo witchcraft.
description: A handwritten book of prayers, charms, and remedies kept by Danish cunning folk, the 'black book' or Cyprianus, named after the apocryphal magician-bishop Cyprianus of Antioch. The books mixed church prayers with healing formulas against disease, worms, and bewitchment. Hundreds survive in Danish archives as evidence of a living folk magic that continued well into the 19th century.

name: Cauldron of the Underjordiske
powers: Lent by the mound folk, who always return what they borrow.
description: In Danish legend the underjordiske, the folk who live inside burial mounds, are said to borrow pots, kettles, and spoons from farmhouses, as when a mound-man calls 'lend me kettle and spoon, while I cook lamb soup under Kovsbakke'. They always return the loan, and breaking their bargains brought trouble. The motif is recorded in Evald Tang Kristensen's collections of Jutland legends.
